section.title: Warning Against Idleness
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from doctrine to daily life. He asks for prayer for the spread of the word and for deliverance, then confidently commends the faithful Lord. The heart of the section is a firm correction of certain idle, disorderly members who have stopped working and become busybodies, over against Paul's own example of hard labor and the plain rule that the unwilling to work should not eat. He closes with careful instructions for loving discipline of the disobedient.
section.thesis: The faithful Lord who strengthens His people also calls them to orderly, productive lives; so the church must lovingly correct idle, disorderly members, hold up the apostolic example of self-supporting labor, refuse to grow weary in doing good, and discipline the disobedient not as enemies but as brothers.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the request for prayer and the confidence in the faithful Lord who guards and directs His people; the command against idleness, grounded in Paul's example and the rule that the unwilling to work should not eat; and the closing instructions to keep doing good and to discipline the disobedient as brothers, not enemies.

units.label: Prayer and the faithful Lord
units.note: for the word to spread and the church to be guarded

verses.text: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may spread quickly and be held in honor, just as it was with you.
And pray that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men; for not everyone holds to the faith.
But the Lord is {{pistos|faithful}}, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
And we have confidence in the Lord that you are doing and will continue to do what we command.
May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance.

units.label: The command against idleness
units.note: the apostolic example and the rule about work

verses.text: Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep away from any brother who leads an {{ataktos|undisciplined}} life that is not in keeping with the {{paradosis|tradition}} you received from us.
For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not undisciplined among you,
nor did we eat anyone's food without paying for it. Instead, in labor and toil, we worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to any of you.
Not that we lack this right, but we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate.
For even while we were with you, we gave you this command: "If anyone is unwilling to {{ergazomai|work}}, he shall not eat."
For we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, but being {{periergazomai|busybodies}}.
We command and urge such people by our Lord Jesus Christ to begin working quietly to earn their own living.

units.label: Do good and discipline as brothers

verses.text: But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing.
Take note of anyone who does not obey the instructions we have given in this letter. Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed.
Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

pistos.gloss: Faithful, trustworthy, reliable. Paul turns from the faithlessness of wicked men in verse 2 to the faithfulness of the Lord in verse 3: not everyone holds to the faith, but the Lord is faithful. God's dependable character is the ground for the promise that He will strengthen and guard His people from the evil one.

paradosis.gloss: Tradition, that which is handed over or passed on. As in chapter two, it means the authoritative apostolic teaching, here including the example and instruction about work that Paul delivered in person. The idle members are living out of step with this received tradition, and so are to be corrected.

ataktos.gloss: Disorderly, undisciplined, idle; originally a military term for a soldier out of rank or a line that has broken formation. It describes members who have abandoned the orderly duty of daily work. The word covers more than laziness: it is a life out of step, disrupting the church's order and burdening others.

ergazomai.gloss: To work, labor, be busy at a task. It anchors Paul's rule that the one unwilling to work should not eat, and his call to the idle to work quietly and earn their own bread. Honest labor is treated as the normal, dignified calling of the believer, and Paul's own night-and-day toil is the model.

periergazomai.gloss: To be a busybody, to meddle, to be busy about the wrong things. Paul coins a deliberate wordplay: the idle are not working, ergazomai, but working around, periergazomai, meddling in others' affairs. Idleness is not neutral; the energy withdrawn from honest labor is spent disturbing the community.

basic.context: Paul closes the letter with practical matters. He asks the church to pray that the gospel would run and that he would be rescued from hostile men, then reassures them that the Lord is faithful to strengthen and guard them. The main concern is a group in the church who have stopped working, are living off others, and have become meddlers. Paul points to his own example of paying his way by hard work, repeats his rule that those unwilling to work should not eat, and tells the idle to get back to quiet, self-supporting labor. Finally he explains how to discipline those who refuse to obey: firmly, but as brothers, not enemies.
basic.hermeneutics: The rule that the unwilling to work should not eat targets those who will not work, not those who cannot; it is not a denial of care for the genuinely needy, whom Scripture everywhere commands us to help. The disorderly problem may have been fed by a distorted view of Christ's return, as if imminence excused ordinary duties. The discipline Paul prescribes aims at restoration, shame that leads to repentance, not rejection.
basic.originalLanguages: The Lord is pistos, faithful, over against faithless men. The problem is the ataktos life, a military image of a soldier out of rank, a disorderly idleness out of step with the paradosis, the apostolic tradition. Paul's rule turns on ergazomai, to work: the unwilling to work should not eat. He coins a pointed wordplay in verse 11: the idle are not working, ergazomai, but periergazomai, working around, meddling as busybodies.
basic.typology: Paul's self-supporting labor and refusal to be a burden reflects the pattern of honest work woven through Scripture from the garden onward, where God gives humanity the dignity of labor. The call not to grow weary in well-doing anticipates the harvest promised to those who persevere in doing good.
basic.christ: The commands are given in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by His authority, showing that even ordinary matters of work and order fall under His lordship. Paul prays that the Lord would direct their hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance, so that the patient endurance of Christ Himself becomes the pattern and power for the church's faithful, orderly life.
basic.god: God is faithful. Against a backdrop of wicked men and internal disorder, the Lord is the one who strengthens His people, guards them from the evil one, and directs their hearts into His love. He is a God of order, not chaos, who dignifies honest work and calls His people to steady, productive, loving lives.
basic.crossReferences: First Thessalonians 4 already urged this church to work with their hands and lead quiet lives. Ephesians 4 tells the former thief to work honestly so as to have something to share. And Galatians 6 says do not grow weary in doing good, for we will reap a harvest, echoed almost exactly here.
basic.oneStory: The gospel produces not only right belief but ordered, generous, hardworking lives. The faithful Lord who guards His people also shapes a community marked by honest labor, mutual care, perseverance in good, and loving discipline, a foretaste of the ordered new creation where God's people serve Him without weariness.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 is the letter's last movement, and it has three parts that are easy to read as unrelated. Verses 1 to 5 ask for prayer and give a prayer. Verses 6 to 15 are the longest sustained command in either Thessalonian letter, and are marked as such by the word 'command' (verses 4, 6, 10, 12). Verses 16 to 18 close. What binds them is the Lord's faithfulness: verse 3 says 'the Lord is faithful,' and verse 5 asks that He 'direct your hearts,' and then the command section applies that faithful strength to a concrete problem.

Inside the command section the writing is carefully arranged. Verse 6 states the command with its authority: 'in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Verses 7 to 9 give the example, the apostle's own life, and verse 10 gives the rule, as a quotation of what he said in person. Verse 11 names the problem, and verse 12 gives the remedy. The way Paul argues is worth noticing: example first, then rule, then diagnosis, then cure. The whole section is also bracketed by a repeated word, 'disorderly' or 'undisciplined' (verses 6, 7 and 11), which runs through it like a thread.

A last literary feature is the word play in verse 11. The idle are 'not working at all but working around,' which in Greek is a pun, ergazomai and periergazomai, 'not busy but busybodies.' The section closes with a turn in the opposite direction: 'do not grow weary in well-doing,' and with the tender instruction in verse 15 to treat the offender 'as a brother.'
context.historical:
The ancient Mediterranean world held a mixed view of manual labor. For many of the elite, work with the hands was beneath a free man, and in a patron and client society a person could expect to receive meals and favors from a wealthier benefactor in return for loyalty. Paul, by contrast, practiced a trade. Acts 18:3 says he worked as a tentmaker, and in Thessalonica itself he worked 'night and day' (1 Thessalonians 2:9). To work for a living in a city like Thessalonica was a visible choice, and Paul made it on purpose: 'to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate.'

The problem in the church probably had more than one cause, and the letter does not pick between them. Some have thought the news of the Lord's nearness led certain believers to stop working, since the world seemed to be ending. That fits the earlier panic over the day of the Lord (2:2), and the first letter already addressed the same issue (1 Thessalonians 4:11 to 12; 5:14). Others have suggested that some had leaned on wealthier members of the church as patrons and took the generosity of the church for granted. Others see a plain case of laziness. Whatever the cause, the result was the same: believers were being supported by the labor of others while spending their time on other people's business, a pattern 1 Timothy 5:13 also describes.

Paul also had a right, which he mentions here, to be supported by the churches in his preaching (1 Corinthians 9:12). He gave it up so that no one could call the gospel a business, and so that the Thessalonians could see a model.
context.canonical:
The Bible treats work as part of God's good design before the fall. Adam is put in the garden 'to cultivate and keep it' (Genesis 2:15), and after the fall the work becomes toil, 'by the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread' (Genesis 3:19). Paul's rule that the unwilling to work should not eat is not new; it takes Genesis 3:19 and turns it into a rule for the church. Proverbs says the same in its own way: 'Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth' (Proverbs 10:4), 'The slacker does not plow in season; at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there' (Proverbs 20:4), and 'Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise' (Proverbs 6:6).

The New Testament carries this through. Paul told the Ephesians that a thief must work 'with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need' (Ephesians 4:28), so that work has a purpose beyond the worker. He told Timothy that the man who does not provide for his household 'has denied the faith' (1 Timothy 5:8). The call to 'not grow weary in well-doing' has a twin in Galatians 6:9, with its promise of a harvest 'in due time.'

On discipline, the passage belongs with a small group of texts: Matthew 18:15 to 17 on confronting a brother, 1 Corinthians 5:11 on not eating with a flagrant sinner who claims to be a brother, Romans 16:17 on turning away from those who cause divisions, and Titus 3:10. Alongside them stands Galatians 6:1, which says to restore the one caught in a trespass 'with a spirit of gentleness.' This passage in 2 Thessalonians is the mildest of the group, and the only one that is explicitly about a lifestyle problem rather than doctrine or gross sin.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted to protect a church from two dangers at once: the harm of those who would not carry their share, and the harm of a harsh response. He opens with prayer and with a promise that God is faithful, because the first need of a troubled church is to look at God before it looks at the offender. Then he gives a very concrete command, and he roots it not in his preferences but in the Lord Jesus' authority.

He did not want the church to settle this with a rule alone. He gives his own life as the pattern: he had a right to support and gave it up, he worked night and day, and he did it so that they would have an example to follow. His method of teaching is to do what he says. The rule 'if anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat' was one he had given in person, so it was not a new burden but a reminder.

Finally Paul wanted the discipline to be restorative. The goal of the withdrawal is 'that he may be ashamed,' meaning that he would come to himself and return. And the offender is never to be treated as an enemy but as a brother. A church that reads this passage correctly will be neither lax nor cold, and will give attention both to the working and to the person who is not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
There is a real mixture here, and it helps to sort it. The description is a report of the problem: some were 'accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies.' The prescriptions are the commands: work quietly, earn your own living, do not grow weary in doing good, take note of those who do not obey, do not associate with them, admonish them as brothers. The apostle's own conduct is offered as an example, not a requirement: he says he had the right to be supported and gave it up, so his waiver of that right is something to imitate in spirit but not a rule that no minister may be paid (compare 1 Corinthians 9:14).

Most of what is commanded still applies to us in principle. The rule about eating is aimed at those who are able and unwilling, not those who are unable. Nothing in this passage permits a church to deny help to the sick, the elderly, the unemployed through no fault of their own, or the widow with no family; elsewhere Scripture requires care for them (1 Timothy 5:3 to 4, Acts 4:34). The withdrawal in verse 14 is also a form of church discipline carried out by the whole church, not by an individual's private disapproval, and it is directed at disobedience to what the letter says, with a restoring purpose.

So the passage describes a specific situation, and a wise application keeps the principles while paying attention to the situation: honest work, a refusal to live off others without need, a disciplined community, and loving restoration.

debates.question: What does 'do not associate with him' in verse 14 require?

views.label: Excommunication from the church
views.case: Some take the words as a formal exclusion, parallel to 1 Corinthians 5:11 and 13, where the church is told not to eat with an unrepentant brother and to 'expel the wicked man.' The verb Paul uses, 'mix with,' is the same in 1 Corinthians 5:9 and 11, and the language of a church-wide act ('take note of him') fits a formal step.

views.label: A limited social withdrawal that keeps him within the fellowship
views.case: Others point out that verse 15 says not to treat him as an enemy but to admonish him as a brother, which implies that he remains a brother and is still in contact with the church. The point is to stop treating his behavior as normal by withdrawing the ordinary comforts of fellowship, such as shared meals, while continuing to speak to him as family.

views.label: A step before formal discipline
views.case: A third view treats this as an early stage in a process like Matthew 18:15 to 17, to be followed by further steps if there is no repentance.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the aim, which is shame leading to repentance, and the manner, which is as to a brother. Wise application starts with gentler steps and escalates only as the situation requires, and never uses discipline as punishment.

debates.question: Why were some of the Thessalonians idle?

views.label: Excitement about the nearness of the Lord's coming
views.case: The letter is about the day of the Lord, and 2:2 mentions a claim that it had come. People who think the end is here may stop planting and building. The first letter's repeated urging to work (1 Thessalonians 4:11 to 12) fits the same pressure.

views.label: Dependence on patrons within the church
views.case: In a society where clients depended on patrons, some may have regarded the church's wealthier members as sources of support and treated their own labor as unnecessary. Paul's language about not being a burden and about earning 'their own living' fits this view.

views.label: Plain disorder and a low view of manual work
views.case: Verses 6 and 11 speak of an 'undisciplined' life, a way of living out of order, and nothing in them need depend on a theory. Some people in every age prefer other people's business to their own work.

debates.bearing: Paul does not settle the cause because the remedy is the same: work quietly and eat your own bread. For us the lesson is that a religious idea, a social habit, or simple laziness can all produce the same fruit, and the cure is the same.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's central word is ataktos, 'undisciplined' or 'disorderly,' and its family appears in verses 6, 7 and 11. The adjective means out of order, and in Greek writing it is commonly used of soldiers who leave their ranks. Paul had already used it in 1 Thessalonians 5:14 ('admonish the unruly'), and here the verb in verse 7, 'we were not undisciplined,' turns it on himself: he lived within the order he asked of them. The word is not about idleness alone but about leaving one's place in the common life. It makes the problem a matter of the church's shared order, not just of private habits.

The contrast in verse 11 is a pun. Paul says some are not ergazomenous but periergazomenous. The first is a participle meaning 'working,' and the second adds peri, 'around,' to make a word that means to be a busybody, working around other people's business. It is a pun in English as well when put as 'not busy but busybodies.' It shows that the idle were not doing nothing; they were occupied with the wrong things.

The rule of verse 10 is carefully worded. 'If anyone is unwilling to work' uses thelei, the verb of willing. The condition is about the will, not about ability. And 'he shall not eat' is a third person imperative, 'let him not eat,' which is an instruction to the church about what it should do, not a prediction of hunger.

There is a word play in verses 8 and 12 as well. In verse 8 Paul says they did not eat bread 'free,' dorean, as a gift. In verse 12 the idle are to 'eat their own bread,' ton heauton arton, which the English renders as 'earn their own living.' Bread is the plain Greek word for daily food. The command is that they eat bread which they have earned. Verse 12 adds that the work is to be done 'with quietness,' meta hesychias, the same quiet life that 1 Thessalonians 4:11 holds up.

The wording for what he and his companions did is 'labor and toil,' kopos and mochthos, 'night and day,' the same pair as in 1 Thessalonians 2:9. The two nouns together stress effort and fatigue.

In verse 14 Paul tells the church to 'take note,' semeiousthe, a verb meaning to mark, and 'not to associate,' synanamignysthai, a compound that means to mix up together with. Paul uses the same compound in 1 Corinthians 5:9 and 11. The verb for what the church does in verse 15 is noutheteo, 'admonish,' from nous, mind, so that the sense is to put in mind. The goal of the withdrawal is entrepo, 'to be turned about, ashamed,' a verb that points to being brought to see.

Finally, verse 3 says 'He will guard you from the evil one,' tou ponerou, which can be read as 'evil' in general or 'the evil one,' as in the Lord's Prayer. Both readings are possible, and the BSB renders it 'the evil one.'

typology.type: Work before the fall, and work after
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 2:15 puts the man in the garden to cultivate and keep it, and Genesis 3:19 makes that work sweat and thorns. Paul's rule 'If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat' is the same word in the church's life: God's order for labor still stands. The correspondence is that human beings were made to work and to eat the result. The escalation is that Christ's people work 'for the Lord and not for men' (Colossians 3:23) and for the sake of sharing (Ephesians 4:28). The type falls short in that work in Genesis is a creation order, while here it is a discipline for a community under grace, and the final rest is still ahead (Hebrews 4:9).

typology.type: Paul as a pattern to imitate
typology.fulfillment: Paul says he offered himself as an example. The Bible often gives a person as a pattern: Israel's patriarchs, the prophets in suffering (James 5:10), and at the center Christ, who left an example that we should follow in His steps (1 Peter 2:21). The correspondence is that Paul's life teaches by showing. The escalation is that Paul's example is itself an echo of Christ's self-giving, as he says elsewhere, 'You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ' (1 Corinthians 11:1). The type falls short because an apostle's example may be copied only in so far as it follows the Lord.

Proverbs 6:6 to 8 tells the 'slacker' to learn from the ant, which prepares in summer and has no commander. Galatians 6:9 and verse 13 here promise a harvest in due time for those who do not grow weary. The correspondence is the farm calendar of sowing, patience and reaping, applied to a life of steady good work. The escalation is that the harvest is no longer only bread but the 'eternal life' of Galatians 6:8, and the work is done 'in the Lord.' The type falls short because Proverbs speaks of wise management of one's own affairs, while the New Testament sets steady labor inside the church's duty to the needy.

The pattern of discipline for a wayward member runs from Israel's laws to Jesus' teaching in Matthew 18:15 to 17, where the aim is to win the brother. The correspondence is a community that takes seriously the harm one person's conduct does to others and acts to turn him back. The escalation in the New Testament is that the one doing the admonishing is guided by 'a spirit of gentleness' (Galatians 6:1) and the example of a Lord who seeks the lost. The type falls short of a method, since Scripture gives principles, not a procedure, for every case.

study.christ:
Christ's presence in this passage is easy to miss, because the topic is work and church order. But look at where Paul places Him. The command in verse 6 is given 'in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,' and the appeal in verse 12 is 'by our Lord Jesus Christ.' Paul does not simply say that this is a good idea or a custom of the apostles; he says it comes with the authority of Jesus. Ordinary matters of daily bread and daily labor are brought under the lordship of the risen Christ. There is no part of life, not even the question of who does the dishes in a household, that stands outside His rule.

The second place is the prayer in verse 5: 'May the Lord direct your hearts into God's love and Christ's perseverance.' The phrase 'Christ's perseverance' can mean the patient endurance that Christ showed, or the patience we need as we wait for Christ, or the endurance Christ gives. Each is true and each fits. The first is the most striking. Jesus' patient endurance is the pattern, since 'for the joy set before Him He endured the cross' (Hebrews 12:2), and He did not give up in the face of opposition. Believers who are tempted to become weary in well-doing are pointed to the One who did not grow weary, and who gives them His own steadiness.

Third, Christ is the pattern for Paul's example. Paul says that he chose not to claim his rights so as to be an example, and elsewhere he says that Christ, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor' (2 Corinthians 8:9). The way of the cross is the way of giving up a right for the sake of others. When Paul labors so as not to burden the church, he is imitating the One who took on the burdens of others. The principle behind the whole passage, that we do not live at the expense of others but for their good, reaches its fullest expression in the Lord who 'did not come to be served, but to serve' (Mark 10:45).

Finally, there is a connection with discipline. The Lord Jesus is the one who told His church how to deal with a brother who sins, and His goal was to win him back (Matthew 18:15). He is also the Shepherd who goes after a lost sheep. A church that treats the idle as 'a brother' and not 'an enemy' is behaving as Christ behaves.
study.god:
The God of this passage is first of all faithful. Verse 3 sets the Lord's faithfulness against the unfaithfulness of 'wicked and evil men' and against the fact that 'not everyone holds to the faith.' The words for 'faith' in verse 2 and 'faithful' in verse 3 share a root in Greek, so there is a play on words: people lack pistis, but the Lord is pistos. The church is surrounded by threats outside, in the hostile men, and weakness inside, in the idle and the disobedient, and the answer to both is that God is who He is. The promise, 'He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one,' is as plain as a promise can be.

God is also a God of order. The word at the heart of the command, ataktos, is the opposite of order, and the God who made the world in an ordered sequence (Genesis 1) is the one who expects His people to live with order. Paul says elsewhere that 'God is not a God of disorder but of peace' (1 Corinthians 14:33). The order He wants is not rigid; it is the order of a family in which each person carries what he can and the weak are helped (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

God dignifies work. Nothing here treats labor as a curse to be escaped. The apostle who preached to cities also made tents, and he speaks of working 'night and day' with no hint of shame. Work is a human way of reflecting the God who worked in creation and who, in Jesus, had a carpenter's trade in the eyes of His neighbors (Mark 6:3). The command to eat one's own bread is a recognition that the Creator made us to produce and to share.

Finally, God is a God of love and discipline together. The prayer in verse 5 asks that hearts be directed 'into God's love,' and the discipline in verses 14 and 15 is meant to be an expression of that love. 'The Lord disciplines the one He loves' (Hebrews 12:6) is the principle behind it. A God who loves disciplines in order to heal.

For worship, this means that the believer can bring the plainest worries to God. The ordinary tasks of the week, the work that is hard to do, and the community that is hard to live in are all places where God is at work. The right response to a disordered church is not despair or harshness, but prayer to the faithful Lord, and then obedience to the commands He has given.

crossReferences.note: 'Aspire to live quietly, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands.' The first letter had already given the same instruction with the same reason, so that they would be dependent on no one. The second letter hardens the tone because the problem has not gone away.

'Admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak.' The word for 'unruly' is the same family as 'undisciplined' in 3:6, and the verse shows that the first response to disorder is admonition, which is also what 3:15 asks.

'Our labor and toil. We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden.' The exact phrase of 3:8, here told as a memory. It shows that Paul's example was public and consistent from the first visit.

The former thief must work 'with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need.' It supplies the purpose of work that 2 Thessalonians 3 assumes: to avoid being a burden, and to be able to give.

'Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest.' Almost the same words as verse 13, with the added promise. It shows that the call is meant for the whole church, not just the idle.
'By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread.' The deep root of the rule in verse 10: bread comes through work, a fact of the world after the fall. Paul applies the principle to the church.

The slacker is sent to the ant, which provides for itself without a commander. It is the wisdom background to Paul's command and shows that the instruction to work is part of long-standing biblical teaching.

Paul had a right to support, but 'we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ.' It explains verse 9, in which he gives up his right for the sake of an example.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders that his own hands ministered to his needs and to those of his companions, so that by such hard work they would help the weak, recalling that 'it is more blessed to give than to receive.' It shows that his labor was meant for generosity.

The man who does not provide for his own household 'has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' It gives the weight Paul attaches to work. Taking care of one's household is a matter of faith, not just economics.

Younger widows 'learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies.' It describes the same pairing of idleness and meddling that verse 11 has in mind, and shows the pattern was a general risk.

'With such a man do not even eat.' A stronger form of the withdrawal in verse 14, for a brother caught in flagrant sin. The comparison shows that 2 Thessalonians 3 is a milder case and is aimed at shame and recovery.

'If someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness.' The tone required for the 'admonish him as a brother' of verse 15, with the added warning to watch yourself.

'Join me in my struggle by praying to God for me.' Paul's request for prayer in 3:1 to 2 follows a habit of asking the churches to pray for rescue from unbelievers, here in Judea, and shows how real the threat of opposition was.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with human beings placed in a garden to cultivate and keep it, and the first lie in that story is that God is holding something back. The fall brought the sweat and the thorns, and since then work has carried both the dignity of the original gift and the weight of the curse. This passage is the apostle's attempt to show what work looks like for people who belong to the new creation, and so it speaks to something the story has been carrying for a long time.

Look at what it answers. When Cain's line and the builders of Babel spent their labor to make a name for themselves, work became a way of self-assertion. When Israel was in Egypt, labor was a form of oppression. In the prophets, laziness and greed alike are condemned, and the ideal is a land where each person sits under his own vine. Here the church is shown a different way: honest work, done quietly, so as to have bread and to have something to give. It is not escape from labor and it is not worship of labor. It is work that is under the lordship of Christ, as an act of love.

Look at what it sets up. The command to work is not for the sake of work alone but so that no one would be a burden, so that the church can support the weak, and so that outsiders see a life that is orderly (1 Thessalonians 4:12). In this way the Christian community becomes a small picture of the kingdom, a place where each gives and receives, and where discipline is for restoration.

And look at how it ends. Believers are told not to grow weary in doing good, because there is a harvest coming. Galatians 6:9 says the harvest comes 'in due time,' and Revelation 14:13 promises that the works of those who die in the Lord follow them. The final picture of the story is a restored garden-city where 'No longer will there be any curse,' and His servants 'will worship Him' (Revelation 22:3). Work is not abolished in the new creation; it is freed from sweat and thorns and joined to rest, so that the labor of God's people is finally joyful.

Until then, the faithful Lord guards His people from the evil one, strengthens them in their ordinary labor, and teaches them to treat even the disorderly as brothers. The community that does this is already living out the end of the story.

quiz.q: What does Paul ask the church to pray for in verses 1 and 2?

options.text: That the word of the Lord would spread and be honored, and that he would be delivered from wicked men.
options.note: Verses 1 and 2 request prayer for the gospel's advance and for deliverance.

options.text: That the church would gain political power in the city.
options.note: Paul prays for the word's spread and his protection, not for political power.

options.text: That all persecution would immediately end forever.
options.note: He asks for deliverance from evil men, but the focus is the word running freely.

options.text: That the idle members would simply be ignored.
options.note: The prayer requests concern the gospel and deliverance; the idle are addressed later, not ignored.

quiz.q: What comfort does Paul give in verse 3, over against faithless men?

options.text: The Lord is faithful and will strengthen and guard the church from the evil one.
options.note: Verse 3 contrasts faithless men with the faithful Lord who guards His people.

options.text: The church must simply defend itself by its own strength.
options.note: It is the Lord who strengthens and guards them, not their own strength alone.

options.text: God will remove every difficult person from their lives at once.
options.note: The promise is protection and strengthening, not the instant removal of all opponents.

options.text: There is no real protection against evil.
options.note: The verse plainly promises the faithful Lord will guard them from the evil one.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the problem with certain members in verses 6 and 11?

options.text: They are living undisciplined, idle lives, not working but becoming busybodies.
options.note: Verses 6 and 11 describe disorderly idleness and meddling.

options.text: They are working too hard and neglecting worship.
options.note: The problem is idleness, not overwork.

options.text: They are giving away too much of their money.
options.note: The issue is refusing to work and meddling, not excessive generosity.

options.text: They are traveling to plant new churches.
options.note: They are accomplishing nothing and meddling, not doing missionary work.

quiz.q: What example did Paul set while he was with them, according to verses 7 to 9?

options.text: He worked night and day and paid his own way, so as not to burden anyone.
options.note: Verses 7 to 9 recount Paul's self-supporting labor as a deliberate example.

options.text: He demanded to be fully supported by the church.
options.note: Though he had that right, he chose to pay his own way as a model.

options.text: He avoided all work to devote himself only to prayer.
options.note: He explicitly worked in labor and toil among them.

options.text: He lived off the wealth of rich patrons.
options.note: He deliberately did not eat anyone's food without paying, unlike relying on patrons.

quiz.q: What rule had Paul given, according to verse 10?

options.text: If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.
options.note: Verse 10 states the rule aimed at the willfully idle.

options.text: No believer should ever earn a wage.
options.note: The rule commends work, not the avoidance of earning.

options.text: Only the wealthy are required to work.
options.note: The rule applies to any who are unwilling to work, not only the wealthy.

options.text: The needy and disabled must fend entirely for themselves.
options.note: The rule targets the unwilling, not those genuinely unable; Scripture commands care for the needy.

quiz.q: How are believers to treat a disobedient brother, according to verses 14 and 15?

options.text: Note him and withhold association so he feels shame, yet admonish him as a brother, not an enemy.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 prescribe restorative discipline that still treats him as a brother.

options.text: Cut him off permanently and treat him as an enemy.
options.note: Paul explicitly says not to regard him as an enemy but to admonish him as a brother.

options.text: Ignore his behavior entirely and say nothing.
options.note: They are to take note and admonish him, not ignore the disobedience.

options.text: Punish him harshly to make an example of him.
options.note: The aim is loving, restorative shame that leads to repentance, not harsh punishment.

questions: Paul turns from faithless men to the faithful Lord who strengthens and guards His people. Where do you need to fix your eyes on the Lord's faithfulness rather than on the unreliable people around you?

The passage treats honest work as a dignified calling and even models paying one's own way. How do you view your daily work, and how might seeing it as service to Christ change your attitude toward it?
Paul warns that idleness turns into meddling; energy withdrawn from good work gets spent on being a busybody. Where might restlessness or avoidance be tempting you to meddle rather than to serve?
The command is not to grow weary in doing good. In what area of well-doing are you tired right now, and what would help you keep going?
Church discipline here is firm yet aims to restore a brother, never to destroy an enemy. How can you hold together honesty about sin and genuine love when someone close to you goes astray?

translationNotes.note: Undisciplined translates ataktos, a military term for a soldier out of rank; it denotes disorderly idleness, a life out of step with the received apostolic tradition.
If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat concerns those who refuse to work, not those unable to; the wider biblical witness commands generous care for the genuinely needy.
The Greek plays on words that English can only approximate: they are not working (ergazomenous) but working around, that is, being busybodies (periergazomenous).
